text: His name was Mahmoud of Ghazni.
Starting around the year 1000,
he raided North India again and again.
About 17 times, he came for gold.
His raiders stripped cities and temples,
including the famous Temple of Somnath in Gujarat in 1026.
Then, he went home.
His camels loaded.
Keep that picture in your mind.
land, India's gold leaving on someone else's camels.
Mahmoud never stayed, but about a hundred and fifty years later another raider from
Afghanistan arrived with a much bigger idea.
He didn't just want India's gold, he wanted India.
His name was Mohammad Avroor, and in 1191 at Tarain near Delhi he ran into the Rajput
King Prithviraj Chauhan. Prithviraj crushed him. Gori was badly wounded, and his own men
carried him off the field. Shall we chase them, your majesty?
Let him go. A man who loses like that doesn't come back.
And if he does? Then we'll beat him again.
Whatever he really said, he didn't finish the job.
A year later, Gori came back. Same battlefield. A bigger, better trained army.
me. This time Prithviraj lost. Rule one of history. If you beat someone, make sure they
don't come back next year.
In 1206, one of Gori's generals became the first Sultan of Delhi, and began the tallest
brick minaret in the world, the Kutub Minar. You can still see it in Delhi today. In these
same years, Nalanda was sacked, and its great libraries were lost.
And here's where our question really begins.
Mahmoud came for the gold and went home.
These newcomers came for the gold and stayed.
For the next 300 years, five different families would rule from Delhi.
And they were about to discover that ruling India was very different from robbing it.
Especially the strangest Sultan of them all.
